title: Expansion, quoting & variables
about: How bash turns a typed line into the words a command receives: quoting, escaping, variables and the environment, wildcards, brace and tilde expansion, command substitution, arithmetic and aliases.

questions.title: Stages of evaluating a command line
questions.text: Put the stages the shell applies to a command line in order.

items.why: The first word may be replaced by an alias.
Values are filled in before the file-name patterns are looked at.

items.t: Expand wildcards such as `*.txt` into file names
items.why: Done on the result of the previous stage.

items.t: Set up redirections, then run the command
items.why: The program finally starts with the final list of words.

questions.title: Who expands the star
questions.text: In `ls *.txt`, who replaces `*.txt` by a list of file names?

options.t: The shell, before `ls` starts; `ls` only sees the resulting names.
options.why: Programs do not do their own globbing.
The kernel knows nothing about patterns.

questions.title: Seeing the final words
questions.text: Which command shows exactly what arguments a command receives after all expansions, one per line?

options.why: It prints each expanded word on its own line.
That only suppresses the final newline.

questions.title: Variable before glob
questions.text: `Y='*.c'; echo $Y` prints the names of the `.c` files of the directory, while `echo "$Y"` prints `*.c`. Why?

options.t: An unquoted `$Y` is expanded first, and its result is then subject to word splitting and wildcard expansion; in double quotes neither happens.
options.why: That is why variables are normally quoted.

options.t: Because double quotes delete the star.
options.why: They keep it as a literal character.

options.t: Because `echo` expands stars only in single quotes.

questions.title: Quoting mechanisms
questions.text: Match each form with its behaviour.

pairs.r: Everything is literal, no expansions at all
pairs.why: Even `$` and backslash are plain characters.

pairs.r: Variables, `$(...)` and arithmetic are expanded; wildcards and word splitting are not
The next character is taken literally
pairs.why: Useful for a single special character.

pairs.r: A string where escapes like `\t` are interpreted
pairs.why: An ANSI-C style string of bash.

questions.title: Single versus double
questions.text: Given `X=world`, what does `echo 'hi $X'` print?

options.t: An error because `$X` is not defined.

questions.title: Double quotes
questions.text: Given `X=world`, what does `echo "hi $X"` print?

options.why: Double quotes still allow variable expansion.
The shell removes the quotes before `echo` sees the word.
The dollar sign is used by the expansion.

questions.title: Quotes join text
questions.text: What does `echo '$X'"$X"` print when `X=world`?

options.why: Two adjacent quoted pieces form a single word: the first literal, the second expanded.
There is no space between the pieces.
The first piece is not expanded.

questions.title: Whitespace and quotes
questions.text: How many arguments does `echo a   b` pass to `echo`, compared with `echo "a   b"`?

options.why: Unquoted blanks separate words; a quoted string is one word and keeps its spaces.

questions.title: Apostrophe in text
questions.text: Which command prints `it's` correctly?

options.why: A single quote inside double quotes is an ordinary character.
The quote after `it` closes the string; the rest is left open.
A backslash does not escape inside single quotes.

questions.title: Backslash in quotes
questions.text: What do `echo 'a\nb'` and `echo "a\nb"` print in bash (with the default `echo`)?

options.t: Both print `a\nb` literally on one line.
options.why: Bash's `echo` does not interpret `\n` unless `-e` is used.

options.t: Both print `a` and `b` on two lines.
The first prints two lines, the second one.
options.why: Neither quoting form turns `\n` into a newline.

questions.title: Interpret escapes
questions.text: Make `echo` print the two words on separate lines: `echo {{0}} 'one\ntwo'`

wrong.why: That removes the trailing newline only.
That *disables* escape interpretation, which is already the default.

questions.title: Dollar sign as text
questions.text: Which command prints the text `$HOME` literally?

options.why: Single quotes or a backslash prevent the expansion.

questions.title: Backslash and newline
questions.text: What is the effect of a backslash at the end of a line in a script?

options.t: It removes the newline, so the command continues on the next line.
It comments out the next line.

options.why: Inside quotes or not, the pair backslash-newline is removed (except within single quotes).

questions.title: Characters the shell treats specially
questions.text: Select the characters that have a special meaning to the shell when unquoted.

questions.title: Assigning a variable
questions.text: Set the variable `NAME` to `Ana`: `NAME{{0}}Ana`
questions.note: No spaces around `=` in a shell assignment.

wrong.why: Pascal-style assignment does not exist in bash.
Spaces around the equals sign make bash think `NAME` is a command.

questions.title: Spaces in an assignment
questions.text: What does `C = 3` do in bash?

options.t: It tries to run a command called `C` with arguments `=` and `3`, and fails with "command not found".
options.why: Assignments must have no spaces around `=`.

questions.title: Using a variable
questions.text: Which command prints the value of `NAME`?

options.why: The dollar sign asks for the value.
An ampersand would start a background job.

questions.title: Braces
questions.text: Why would you write `${NAME}_backup` instead of `$NAME_backup`?

options.t: Without braces the shell reads the variable name as `NAME_backup` (letters, digits and underscores), which is probably not defined.
options.why: Braces mark where the name ends.

options.t: Braces make the expansion happen earlier.

options.why: The difference is exactly the name boundary.

questions.title: Variables you always have
questions.text: Match each predefined variable with its content.

pairs.why: Usually set by the login process.

questions.title: Exporting
questions.text: What is the difference between `FOO=1` and `export FOO=1`?

options.t: With `export`, the variable is passed to child processes (programs started afterwards); without it the variable stays local to the current shell.
options.why: The environment is inherited, shell variables are not.

options.t: `export` saves the variable in a file for the next login.

options.why: A child only sees exported variables.

questions.title: Child sees nothing
questions.text: After `FOO=local` (no export), what does `bash -c 'echo "[$FOO]"'` print?

options.why: The child shell does not inherit a variable that was not exported.
The value is empty, not the name.
An unset variable expands to an empty string.

questions.title: Temporary variable
questions.text: What does `BAR=tmp bash -c 'echo "[$BAR]"'` print, and what is `$BAR` afterwards in the current shell?

options.t: `[tmp]`, and afterwards `$BAR` is unchanged (empty if it was unset).
options.why: A prefix assignment lives only for that command's environment.

options.t: An error because assignments cannot precede commands.

questions.title: Changes in a subshell
questions.text: After `X=outer; (X=inner; echo $X); echo $X`, what is printed?

options.why: The parentheses create a subshell; its changes are lost when it ends.
Inside the subshell the new value is used.

options.t: An error, since variables cannot be redefined.

questions.title: Environment commands
questions.text: Match each command with what it does.

pairs.r: Prints the value of one exported variable
pairs.why: Exit status 1 if it is not set.

pairs.r: Prints all shell variables and functions
Lists exported variables in a re-usable form

extras.r: Deletes the file with the same name

questions.title: printenv versus echo
questions.text: You ran `FOO=x` (no export). What do `echo $FOO` and `printenv FOO` show?

options.t: `x` for the first; nothing for the second, because `printenv` shows only exported variables.
options.why: A quick test for whether a variable is exported.
`printenv` reads the environment, not shell variables.
The shell variable has a value.

questions.title: Modifying PATH
questions.text: Which line adds `~/bin` to the end of the command search path for this session and its children?

options.why: Keeps the old value and appends the new directory.
Replaces the whole search path, so `ls` is no longer found.
The `&` runs the assignment in a background subshell, which has no effect on your shell.

questions.title: Breaking PATH
questions.text: After `PATH=/nonexistent`, which commands still work?

options.why: A word with a slash is used as a path; no `PATH` search is needed.
Builtins are part of the shell and never consult `PATH`.
It is searched in `PATH`, which no longer lists its directory.
Also an external program searched in `PATH`.

questions.title: Order of search in PATH
questions.text: `PATH=/usr/local/bin:/usr/bin` and both directories contain `tool`. Which one runs?

options.t: The one in `/usr/local/bin`, because the directories are searched from left to right and the first match wins.
options.why: That is how you can override a system program.

options.t: Bash asks which one to run.

questions.title: Delete a variable
questions.text: Remove the variable `FOO` from the shell: `{{0}} FOO`
questions.note: After `unset FOO`, `printenv FOO` fails with status 1.

questions.title: Wildcards
questions.text: Match each wildcard with what it matches in a file name.

pairs.r: Any string of characters, including none
One character in the range 0 to 3

extras.r: One or more repetitions of the previous item
extras.why: That is a regex `+`, not a glob.

questions.title: practica glob
questions.text: Which files does `practica[0-3].c` match, given `practica0.c`, `practica3.c`, `practica4.c`, `practica10.c`?

options.why: One digit from 0 to 3 between `practica` and `.c`.
`4` is outside the range and `10` has two digits.

questions.title: Hidden files and star
questions.text: Does `ls *.dat` list a file named `.hid.dat`?

options.t: No: a leading dot must be matched explicitly, so `*` does not match hidden files.
Yes, but it prints a warning.
options.why: It is not listed at all.

questions.title: No match
questions.text: In a directory with no `.nomatch` files, what does `echo *.nomatch` print by default?

options.why: A pattern with no match is left as it is (unless the `nullglob` option is set).

questions.title: Quoted star
questions.text: What does `echo "*.dat"` print?

questions.title: Names with spaces
questions.text: A directory has `sp ace.dat`. Why might `rm *.dat` still work correctly even though the name has a space?

options.t: Wildcard expansion produces one word per matching file name, so the space does not split the name; the problem arises with *unquoted variables*, not with globs.
options.why: The safe habit is `rm -- *.dat` and always quoting variables.
`rm` receives a separate argument for each name.

options.t: Because the shell adds quotes to the output of `echo`.
It does not; the command fails.

questions.title: Brace expansion
questions.text: Match each brace expression with its expansion.

extras.r: every file that matches a or b
extras.why: Braces do not look at the file system.

questions.title: Brace versus glob
questions.text: What is the difference between `echo {a,b}.dat` and `echo [ab].dat`?

options.t: The brace version always prints `a.dat b.dat`, whether or not the files exist; the glob prints only the existing files that match.
The glob always prints both names.
The brace version needs the files to exist.
options.why: It does not look at the file system.

questions.title: Handy brace use
questions.text: Which command creates a backup copy of `config.ini` as `config.ini.bak` with the least typing?

options.why: A bracket would match one character.
A single item in braces does not expand.

questions.title: Tilde
questions.text: What does `echo ~root` print, and what does `echo "~root"` print?

options.why: The tilde is expanded only when unquoted.

options.t: The current user's home in both cases.

questions.title: Command substitution
questions.text: What does `echo "Today: $(date +%F)"` do?

options.t: It runs `date +%F` first and puts its output into the string.
options.why: The command inside `$(...)` is replaced by what it prints.
That would be the result with single quotes.

options.t: It stores the date in a variable called `Today`.

questions.title: Backticks
questions.text: How do `` `cmd` `` and `$(cmd)` differ?

options.t: They do the same thing, but `$(...)` nests more easily and is more readable.
options.why: The backtick form is the older syntax.

options.t: Backticks run the command in the background.
Backticks print the command instead of running it.

questions.title: Trailing newlines
questions.text: What happens to the newlines at the end of a command's output in `$(cmd)`?

options.t: They are removed from the end; newlines inside the output remain (when quoted).
options.why: So `X=$(date)` does not keep a final newline.

options.t: All newlines are removed, even inside.
options.why: Only trailing ones, unless the expansion is unquoted and word splitting joins lines with spaces.
Literal backslash sequences are not created.

questions.title: Lines in substitution
questions.text: `echo "$(echo a; echo b)" | wc -l` prints 2, while `echo $(echo a; echo b) | wc -l` prints 1. Why?

options.t: Unquoted, the result is split into words that `echo` joins with spaces on one line; quoted, the newline is preserved.
The second form does not run `echo a`.
Quoting changes the output of the inner `echo`.
options.why: It changes how the outer command receives it.

questions.title: Counting with substitution
questions.text: Which command stores the number of entries of the current directory in `N`?

options.why: The output of the pipeline is captured.
That is a pipeline: the assignment runs in its own subshell and is lost, and `wc -l` just waits for keyboard input.
Writes the number into a file called `N`.
Stores the text of the command.

questions.title: Arithmetic tools
questions.text: Match each command with its result.

extras.why: Without a tool, `echo 5+3` prints the text.

questions.title: Text, not numbers
questions.text: What does `A=25; B=4; echo $A*$B+5` print?

options.why: Variables hold text, and `echo` just prints it: no arithmetic happens.
The star stays literal when no file matches; nothing fails.

questions.title: Arithmetic expansion
questions.text: Compute `DATOA*DATOB+5` with the shell itself: `echo {{0}}`
questions.note: Inside `$(( ))` variable names need no dollar sign.

wrong.why: Single parentheses mean command substitution, which would try to run a command called `DATOA*DATOB+5`.

questions.title: expr and the star
questions.text: Multiply in `expr`: `expr 25 {{0}} 4`
questions.note: `'*'` also works; `expr` needs the star escaped or quoted.

wrong.why: The shell expands the unquoted star into file names before `expr` runs.

questions.title: Octal trap
questions.text: What does `echo $((010))` print?

options.why: A leading zero makes the number octal in arithmetic expansion.

questions.title: Integer division
questions.text: What does `echo $((-7/2))` print in bash?

options.why: The shell has no floating point.

questions.title: Increment
questions.text: After `i=1`, what does `echo $((i++)) $i` print?

options.why: Post-increment returns the old value, then increases `i`.

questions.title: What an alias is
questions.text: What is an alias?

options.t: A shorthand the shell substitutes for the first word of a command, such as `alias ll='ls -l'`.
options.why: It is text replacement done early in the evaluation.

options.t: A second name for a file on disk.
A variable that can be exported.
A stored script that runs at login.

questions.title: Alias commands
questions.text: Match each command with what it does.

pairs.r: Reports that `ll` is an alias for `ls -l`
pairs.why: A way to check what a name means.

questions.title: Keeping an alias
questions.text: You defined `alias rm='rm -i'` in a terminal. When will it be available again after you close the terminal?

options.t: Only if the definition is written to `~/.bashrc` (or another startup file).
options.why: Aliases live in the shell's memory.

options.t: Always, because aliases are stored on disk.
Only in the terminals that are already open.
options.why: New ones will not have it either.

questions.title: Bypassing an alias
questions.text: `rm` is aliased to `rm -i`. Which way runs the real `rm` without the alias for one command?

options.why: A quoted or escaped first word is not alias-expanded.
The alias still applies and adds `-i`.
Needs a name, and removes the alias for the session.

questions.title: Alias and scripts
questions.text: Why might an alias defined in your `~/.bashrc` not work inside a script?

options.t: Non-interactive shells running scripts do not expand aliases by default (and do not read `~/.bashrc`).
options.why: Use functions or full commands in scripts.

options.t: Aliases are deleted when `chmod +x` is run.
